doc.title: Laurence Juber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Glasgow, Scotland, July 27, 2016 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Choosing Goldsmiths over Leeds; Stanley Glasser and learning to sight read
summary: He cancelled Leeds, took a gap year, and entered Goldsmiths where Stanley Glasser championed him; he learned to read from Bert Weedon's book at 11.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: stepchild of that whole world. And still to this day it’s somewhat that way. So when I got better grades than I expected I said wait a minute, why am I going to leave London? I grew up in London and I’d been paying my dues as a teenager and getting demo sessions and playing with all these cats, why do I want to leave all that? So I canceled my application to Leeds, took a gap year — I was a pioneer of the gap year. I mean this was like 1971. And I applied to Goldsmith’s College, London University, which was the only place in London that you could actually study musicology and music theory and all of that within a degree structure that didn’t require being basically a church organist that could improvise fugues in three parts with hands and feet and do all that stuff. Because there was still that kind of church music thrust in music education. And Stanley Glasser, who was the professor at Goldsmith’s, I went in for my interview and we spent the whole time talking about Barney Kessel and Joe Pass, and American jazz guitar players. Because he understood the nature of my world. And he was my champion at Goldsmith’s. I mean for ear training for example. I was not that great at transcribing when it would be like Schoenberg’s F# minor string quartet, stuff like that.

Sight singing I was okay. Because I could sight read. I learned to sight read on a rainy afternoon when I was 11 years old. I had a book called Play in the Day. Burt Weedon’s Play in the Day. I mean you talk to anybody from that generation, they all learned out of Play in the Day. And in the back of the book was “When the Saints Go Marching in” and it’s in C and okay, that’s a C, that’s a C, I get it. It wasn’t rocket science.
